latin.689: GAR. Cum poena proprie dicta sit vindicatio peccati ex instituto legis a legitimo iudice posita: oportet sane poenas omnes peccati, quae in omnes homines ab Adamo prognatos hactenus incubuerunt, & ad finem usque saeculorum incubiturae sunt, secundum alicuius legis denunciationem esse a Deo inflictas, & porro infligendas. Est autem mors quam omnes iam ab initio mundi homines inierunt, poena peccati ex propria sua natura & conditione. Itaque ab initio omnibus inflictam fuisse consentaneum est, iuxta declarationem alicuius legis antea constitutae. At haec non alia invenietur, quam quae Adamo posita est, & obedientiam ab eo sub diserta mortis comminatione postulavit; cum ab Adamo usque ad Mosen nulla legatur alia lex universalis, quae poenas transgressoribus minetur ac denunciet.
latin.690: PLAC. Praeterquam quod haec ratio est superioris responsionis Viri docti confutatio, laborat triplici falsitate. Primo falsum est poenas omnes peccati, quae in omnes homines ab Adamo prognatos hactenus incubuerunt, & ad finem usque saeculorum incubiturae sunt, fuisse vindicationem peccati ex instituto legis a legitimo iudice positam. Id patet ex eo quod pleraeque eiusmodi poenae non minus infliguntur piis, pro quibus Christus plenissime iustitiae & legi satisfecit, quam impiis.
latin.691: Deinde falsum est omnes illas poenas secundum alicuius legis denunciationem esse a Deo inflictas. Quae enim legis denunciatio iubebat infligi Evae multiplicationem dolorum conceptus & partus, & Adamo hanc poenam, ut in sudore vultus sui vesceretur pane, & terra proferret illi spinas & tribulos &c.? Tertio falsum est nullam aliam legem universalem generi humano ab Adamo usque ad Mosen positam fuisse, quae poenas transgressoribus minetur ac denunciet, praeter illam quae obedientiam ab Adamo sub diserta mortis comminatione postulavit. Nam ut omittam legem universalem latam Gen. ix. de homicidio, & de sanguine, nonne ipsi Adamo & toti generi humano lata est lex naturae, quam Apostolus urget Rom. i. & 2.?
latin.692: Denique ut taceam alia vitia, quae in hoc Viri docti argumento deprehendi possunt, aberratio est a statu quaestionis. Non enim nego poenas peccati Adami pertinere ad eius posteros, quia nempe ad eos peccatum Adami pertinet. Communicavit enim nobiscum Adamus per generationem carnalem peccatum suum, & per peccatum, poenas. Per unum hominem peccatum ingressum est in mundum, & per peccatum mors. Fateor etiam propagatum in nos peccatum originale dignum esse mortis supplicio, cum sit vere peccatum repugnans legi naturae, immo omni legi divinae. Haec inter nos controversa esse non debent.
latin.693: Sed quaerebatur de imputatione primi Adae peccati actualis antecedente seu immediata, omnibus Adae posteris, secundum quam legem fiat? Si fiat secundum aliquam legem seu legis denunciationem, non potuit non fieri quin lex illa violaretur; cur igitur eam imputationem Vir doctus liberae Dei voluntati ascribit passim?
latin.694: Si non fiat secundum aliquam legem, quomodo est actio iudiciaria, & punitur sic imputatum illud peccatum, ut legi & iustitiae satisfiat? Nulla enim lex ut sic imputaretur, & imputatum puniretur, exigebat.

pass_a.689: Garissoles: a proper penalty is sin’s vindication set by law through a lawful judge. So every penalty that has lain and will lie on Adam’s line must be inflicted by God under some law’s denunciation. Death, which all have entered from the world’s start, is by its nature a sin-penalty—so from the start it fits some prior law’s declaration. No other universal law from Adam to Moses threatens transgressors except the ban that demanded Adam’s obedience under an express death threat.
pass_a.690: Placeus: besides confuting the prior reply, this reason has a triple falsehood. First: not all those Adam-line penalties were legal vindication by a lawful judge—clear because many fall on the pious, for whom Christ fully satisfied justice and law, no less than on the impious.
pass_a.691: Second: not all were inflicted under some law’s denunciation—what law ordered Eve’s multiplied birth-pains, or Adam’s bread in sweat and thorns? Third: it is false that from Adam to Moses no other universal law threatened penalties besides the death-ban. Omit Gen 9 on homicide and blood: was not nature’s law given to Adam and the whole race, which Paul presses in Rom 1–2?
pass_a.692: Finally, waving other flaws, this wanders from the question’s state. Placeus does not deny Adam’s sin-penalties reach his posterity, because Adam’s sin reaches them. Adam shared his sin with us by fleshly generation, and by sin the penalties: through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death. He also grants propagated original sin deserves death, being true sin against nature’s law—indeed every divine law. That should not be disputed between them.
pass_a.693: But the question was antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam’s first actual sin to all his posterity—by what law? If by some law or denunciation, that law must have been violated; why then does the learned man ascribe that imputation everywhere to God’s free will?
pass_a.694: If it is not by any law, how is it a judicial act, and how is that imputed sin punished so as to satisfy law and justice? For no law required that it be so imputed, and the imputed sin so punished.

689: GAR. Since a penalty properly so called is the vindication of sin set from the institution of a law by a lawful judge: it must indeed be that all the penalties of sin which have thus far lain upon all men sprung from Adam, and will lie to the end of the ages, have been inflicted by God—and are still to be inflicted—according to the denunciation of some law.
But death, which all men have already entered from the beginning of the world, is a penalty of sin by its own nature and condition.
Therefore it is fitting that it was inflicted on all from the beginning, according to the declaration of some law constituted beforehand.

But this will be found to be no other than that which was set for Adam, and demanded obedience from him under an express threat of death; since from Adam to Moses no other universal law is read which threatens and denounces penalties to transgressors.
690: PLAC. Besides the fact that this reason is a confutation of the learned man’s prior reply, it labors under a triple falsehood.

First, it is false that all the penalties of sin which have thus far lain upon all men sprung from Adam, and will lie to the end of the ages, were the vindication of sin set from the institution of a law by a lawful judge.
That is plain from this: that most such penalties are inflicted no less on the pious, for whom Christ has most fully satisfied justice and the law, than on the impious.
691: Next, it is false that all those penalties were inflicted by God according to the denunciation of some law.

For what denunciation of a law ordered that Eve be struck with the multiplication of the pains of conception and birth, and Adam with this penalty—that in the sweat of his face he should eat bread, and that the earth should bring forth thorns and thistles for him, and the rest?

Third, it is false that no other universal law was set for the human race from Adam to Moses which threatens and denounces penalties to transgressors, besides that which demanded obedience from Adam under an express threat of death.
For—to omit the universal law given in Gen. 9 on homicide and on blood—was not the law of nature given to Adam himself and to the whole human race, which the Apostle presses in Romans 1 and 2?
692: Finally, to pass over other faults that can be caught in this argument of the learned man, it is a wandering from the state of the question.
For I do not deny that the penalties of Adam’s sin reach his posterity, because of course Adam’s sin reaches them.
For Adam communicated his sin to us through carnal generation, and through sin, the penalties.
Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death.
I also confess that original sin propagated into us is worthy of the punishment of death, since it is truly sin opposing the law of nature—nay, every divine law.
These things ought not to be disputed between us.
693: But the question was about the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam’s first actual sin to all Adam’s posterity: according to what law does it take place?

If it takes place according to some law or denunciation of a law, it could not but be that that law was violated; why then does the learned man ascribe that imputation everywhere to the free will of God?
694: If it does not take place according to some law, how is it a judicial act, and how is that imputed sin so punished that law and justice are satisfied?
For no law required that it be so imputed, and that the imputed sin be punished.
